title: Way of the Warrior Kid Review: Chris Pratt Overshadows a Young Hero
excerpt:
Variety argues the star's presence distracts from the child's journey.
The family drama struggles to balance its two emotional arcs.
body_md:
Way of the Warrior Kid, directed by McG and adapted from Jocko Willink's book, follows a bullied teenager and his injured military-veteran uncle as both try to recover a sense of confidence. Variety's review argues that the film has worthwhile ideas but struggles to reconcile its family-friendly message with the demands of a star vehicle for Chris Pratt.

Jude Hill plays Marc, a boy who faces persistent bullying at school. Pratt portrays Jake, a decorated Navy SEAL recovering from injuries sustained during a dangerous mission. Jake stays with his sister Sarah, played by Linda Cardellini, in San Diego. When Marc asks his uncle to train him, Jake introduces exercise and discipline while emphasizing that genuine strength can also mean avoiding a fight.

The premise gives the film two potential emotional journeys. Marc needs confidence and a healthier way to respond to intimidation, while Jake is confronting pain and unresolved memories of a mission gone wrong. The review finds that screenwriter Will Staples often handles these ideas too literally, spelling out lessons about courage, loss and resilience instead of allowing them to emerge organically.

At 106 minutes, the adaptation sometimes feels pulled between what young viewers might find meaningful and what adults are expected to appreciate. The critic particularly praises moments that inhabit Marc's perspective, including sequences involving his enthusiasm for video games and his awkward efforts to connect with peers. These grounded passages offer a more convincing view of adolescence than the film's increasingly elaborate later developments.

Cardellini is credited with bringing feeling to the role of a single mother, though the review argues that the character is given too little space. Hill is seen as promising but occasionally directed toward a strangely adult delivery. The central criticism concerns Pratt: his established screen persona and the film's attention to Jake risk pushing Marc, supposedly the story's true protagonist, into the background.

The review draws a comparison with The Karate Kid, where life lessons arise from apparently simple actions. In the critic's assessment, Way of the Warrior Kid lacks that subtlety and sometimes trades emotional credibility for spectacle. This is one published critical opinion rather than an objective verdict; viewers looking for a motivational family story may respond differently to the material.
